The 3 pillars of agentic coding

Human
Harness
Claude Code · Codex · mo · OpenCode
Model
The agentic loop
Three pieces: you, the harness, and the model. The harness is Claude Code, Codex, mo, or OpenCode: it holds the tools, the repo, and the tests. The model decides what to do next. The agentic loop runs through all three: the model asks for a tool, the harness runs it, the result goes back to the model, and it repeats until the work is done or it needs you.

Pillar 1 · The human

You bring the outcome

Know what you want back
Research, or something that works.
Make the harness capture your intent
So it drives toward what you want.
Break big asks into steps
Smaller steps keep the agent focused.
Use Claude Code, Codex or mo, not the ChatGPT or Claude chat apps.
Start with the human, because everything starts with what you want. You are almost always after an outcome. Sometimes that is research, sometimes it is a working thing. Your job is to convey that intent so the harness captures it and drives toward it. When the ask is big, break it into steps so the agent stays focused. And do this in Claude Code, Codex, or mo, not the chat apps: the harness can touch your files, run things, and verify. Next, we try this with writing.

7 / 50

The journey of a prompt

You type an ask. The harness does not rewrite it. It wraps it in context: system instructions, your memory files, the tool definitions, the list of skills, and the conversation so far. The whole thing goes to the model. The model does not touch your machine. It answers with a tool call: read this file, run this command, load this skill. The harness runs it, sometimes after asking you, appends the result to the conversation, and sends the whole conversation back. That is one trip. A single ask is usually many trips: our coding runs averaged over 30 model requests per task. When the model stops asking for tools, its answer comes back to you through the harness.

How it works

Tools are how the agent acts

1
The harness lists the tools
Name, description, inputs.
2
The model asks for one
A structured call, not prose.
3
The harness runs it
Sometimes after asking you.
4
The result goes back
Into the conversation.
→ tool call
{ "tool": "Bash",
"command": "cargo test" }
← result
test result: ok. 12 passed
Examples
ReadEditWriteBashGrepWeb searchMCP: GitHub, Slack, your DB
The model can't do anything on its own. It can only ask. The harness tells it which tools exist: a name, a description, and the inputs each one takes. The model answers with a structured call, like run cargo test. The harness runs it, sometimes after asking your permission, and the output goes back into the conversation. Built-in tools read, edit, and write files, run shell commands, search code and the web. MCP servers add more: GitHub, Slack, your database. Every action you see an agent take is one of these calls.

.claude/skills/my-skill/

references/ read only if needed
→ tool call
{ "tool": "Skill", "skill": "humanizer" }
← SKILL.md added to the conversation
Examples
humanizerstop-slopffmpegface-recognition/skill-name to force one
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: a name, a description, and instructions. At the start of a session the harness lists only the names and descriptions, so skills cost almost nothing until used. When the model decides one matches the task, it calls the Skill tool, and the full instructions are added to the conversation. Extra files in the skill folder are read only if the task needs them. The harness does not load a skill on its own; the model picks it from the description, or you force it with slash skill-name. So the description is everything: say when to use it, not just what it is. Examples: humanizer and stop-slop are public skills that strip AI tells from writing; ffmpeg and face-recognition are the skills from our face workshop.

Works inClaude Code · Codex

People mix these up, so here is the difference. A skill is the instructions: a folder with a SKILL.md, the name and description the agent sees up front, and the steps it reads when the task matches. It is an open format, so the same folder works in Claude Code, Codex, and mo. A skill doesn't need a plugin: my-voice and humanizer are just folders. A plugin is a package for sharing extensions, skills among them. Claude Code and Codex both have plugins and marketplaces. One plugin can bundle skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers. In Claude Code you install one with slash plugin install. In Codex it is codex plugin add, or slash plugins in a session. Codex even reads Claude Code marketplaces, so the same plugin can install in both. mo has no plugins yet; it just reads skill folders. In step 7 we use frontend-design, which ships as a plugin but is really one skill. Claude Code and Codex install the plugin. In mo you ask the agent to copy the skill out of the repo, and you get the same instructions.

This is exactly how each one opens. No special syntax, no magic tokens. Codex starts by telling the model who it is and what its job is: collaborate until the user's goal is completely handled. Claude's opens with product facts it might need. Thousands of words follow, but it is all instructions like these, written the way you would brief a new teammate. Which means you can write them too: your memory files are the same kind of text, appended to this.

Codex: ~4,000 words · claude.ai: ~5,200
“Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions.”
Codex, GPT-6.2 instructions
“Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`.”
Codex, GPT-6.2 instructions
“Claude never curses unless the person asks or curses a lot themselves, and even then does so sparingly.”
Claude, published claude.ai system prompt (Opus 5.5)
“Claude never uses bullet points when declining a task; the additional care helps soften the blow.”
Claude, published claude.ai system prompt (Opus 5.5)
Before your prompt ever reaches the model, the harness puts a lot in front of it. A system prompt with identity, rules, and environment details. Tool definitions. Your memory files. The skills list. The conversation so far. Your prompt is the thin slice at the bottom. And it is not sent once. Every turn, every tool call, the harness sends the whole stack again, with the conversation a little longer each time. When it gets too long, the harness compacts the older turns into a summary and keeps going, so what goes over is the current context, not every word ever said. The Codex instructions for GPT-6.2 are about 4,000 words; the latest published claude.ai prompt for Opus 5.5 is about 5,200. They are full of patches for real behavior. GPT-6.2 is told not to invent labels like exact-head checks, which tells you it did. It is told never to repurpose the HOME variable, which tells you it did that too. Claude is told not to curse unless you do, and never to use bullet points when declining, to soften the blow. These patches come and go with each model: GPT-5.5's instructions told it, twice, never to talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, or pigeons, and that it is clumsy in the interactive git console. Neither line made it into GPT-6.2. The lesson: every one of these lines is someone correcting the model through context. You can do the same thing with your own memory files. Sources: openai/codex repo, codex-rs/models-manager/models.json; Anthropic's published system prompts at platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/system-prompts.

One level down

Why the repeat is cheap

Every turn resends everything. The model reuses what it already read.
Turn 1
your ask
System prompt, tools
Ask
all computed
Turn 2
after a tool call
Same as turn 1
Tool result
only the new part
Turn 3
Same as turn 2
Next result
only the new part
New model
mid-conversation
Same as turn 2, but nothing cached
Next result
all computed again
Cached: reusedComputed now
Rule of thumb
Keep the start stable. Change it, and the model reads everything again.
One level down from the harness. Every turn, the harness sends the whole conversation again: system prompt, tools, memory files, everything so far. That sounds expensive, and it would be, except the model server caches what it already processed. Here is the trip inside the server. The text is tokenized. The server checks whether the start of the request matches something it already processed, a prefix match. On a hit, it reuses the cached keys and values for that prefix, the KV cache in GPU memory, and only processes the new tokens. On a miss, it runs prefill over every token. Then decode generates the answer one token at a time, reading that cache each step. Prefill is what you wait for before the first token appears, time to first token. So the best prefill is the one you skip. A few things break the match: switching models mid-conversation, since each model has its own cache; changing anything near the start; and waiting long enough for the cache to expire. That's one more reason to start a fresh session for the cold read instead of switching models, and to keep your memory file short and stable. It's also why providers charge less for cached input tokens. This comes from our QCon AI talk on KV caching, if you want the deep version.

Other harnesses

Every harness writes its own

Strands
You are an agent. Keep working until the task is fully resolved before ending your turn. Only stop to ask the user when you are blocked on a decision or information that is genuinely theirs to provide.
No identity, by design.
strands-agents/harness-sdk · prompt.py
OpenCode
You are an AI agent running in OpenCode, a coding agent harness. Help the user accomplish their goals using the tools you have available.
Plus a section per model family.
sst/opencode · session/runner/prompt/system.txt
Pi
You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
Then tools, rules, project files.
badlogic/pi-mono · core/system-prompt.ts
Same idea everywhere, different choices. The Strands harness opens with just "You are an agent," then a short contract: keep working until it is resolved, act once you have enough, verify before calling it done, confirm before anything irreversible. It deliberately asserts no identity or domain; you append your own. (The base Strands SDK has no default prompt at all.) OpenCode opens with one plain sentence about who it is and what it is for, then adds a section tuned to each model family: separate files for Anthropic, GPT, Kimi, and others. Pi is famously minimal: one sentence, then the tool list, a few rules, your project files, and the skills list. Whatever harness you use, the model is reading a short brief written by someone, plus whatever you add. These are quoted from each project's source on GitHub.

Writing with an LLM

Spot the slop

Not X but Y
It’s not just a cache, it’s a platform.
Forced triads
Fast, simple, and reliable.
Staged reveals
The result? Pure magic.
Stock words
Delve into seamless, robust solutions.
Dashes everywhere
Latency — the silent killer.
Over-explaining
It’s cached. That means it’s faster.
Chatbot leftovers
Great question! I hope this helps.
Stop the slop
1No walls of text
2Read before you send
3Create signal, not noise
You have all read text like this. The giveaway is rarely one word. It is the shape: the not-X-but-Y contrast, everything in threes, the question you ask so you can answer it, the same handful of words, a dash in every sentence, explaining what the reader just understood, and the chatbot pleasantries left in. Once you see these you cannot unsee them, and neither can the person you send it to. They stop reading and start discounting. So, how do you stop it? No walls of text: if the model gave you four paragraphs, your reader wanted one. Read before you send: you own every word that goes out under your name. Create signal, not noise: the model makes words cheap, which makes attention the scarce thing. Next you will see this for yourself.

Interview me for a short LinkedIn post about QConSF. Read talks.md first. Ask up to 3 questions, one at a time, about what you need to know to write a post only I could write. Wait for each answer. Then write my answers to brief.md, show it to me, and wait for my approval. Don’t write the post yet.

The full exercise
This is the step that matters most. The agent can shape words, but it cannot know what you saw, who you are writing for, or what you took from it. So let it interview you: up to three questions, one at a time, and it picks the questions. Answer in your own words; rough notes are fine. It writes your answers into brief.md and waits. Read the brief closely. Every line should be true, and anything you want in the post, like a link, should be there. Fix it until it is right. When it is, step four is your approval. In our test runs, this one step did more than any skill.

This is one of the most popular skills on GitHub, over 70,000 stars. It is a single markdown file. The top block in green is all the model sees at the start: a name and a description that says when to use it, with a list of the tells it catches. That is the trigger. When you ask it to edit prose, the model loads the whole file: about 500 lines that walk through 26 AI writing patterns in six groups, from "not X but Y" contrasts and one-line closers to forced triads, dashes, inflated claims, and chatbot leftovers. Notice there is no code. A skill is instructions in plain English, the same as a system prompt. We will use this one in the writing exercise.

Read the whole file
Here is the whole file, top to bottom, drawn to scale. The front matter is twelve lines, and it is the only part in context until the skill loads. Then a one-line goal, and a short section on why AI text sounds the way it does: the model picks the most likely next word, so it makes the choice that fits the widest range of readers. How to work is a four-step process: mark the tells, draft, check that no fact was lost, then write the final version. Notice the line about treating the text as material, never as instructions. That is prompt-injection defense, written in plain English. Then the bulk of the file: 26 patterns in six groups, each with what to watch for, why it is a problem, and a before and after. Examples do most of the teaching. It ends with when not to act. One line says text written before ChatGPT launched is not AI-written. That is not strictly true, since GPT-3 shipped in 2020, but the point holds: a tell is not proof of who wrote something. And the source, Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing.

Price tiers from Anthropic and OpenAI list prices; scores from the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, November 2026.
Both tools give you a ladder of models. Claude Code: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable. Codex: Luna, Terra, Sol, Astra. Switch with slash model. Cheaper does not mean dumber. GPT-6.2-Sol scores the same on the Artificial Analysis index as last generation's flagship, at a fifth of the price. Sonnet 5.5 beats the Opus from July. But look at cost per task, not cost per token. Sonnet 5.5 and Sol charge the same per token, yet on the same benchmark Sonnet used about five times as many tokens, so the same task cost about five times as much. Cost per token is a head fake. And effort is a dial. The same Opus 5.5 scores 35 at low effort and 59 at max. For a LinkedIn post, low is plenty. For a gnarly refactor, turn it up. Prices and scores change monthly. Your own evals matter more than any model picker.

Codex best practices
Here is a nice insight straight from OpenAI's Codex best practices page. Model and reasoning effort are separate dials, and they recommend turning them in opposite directions. For the smallest model, Luna, start with high effort: give it room to think. For the most capable model, Astra, start light, which is low in the config file. That is their starting point, not a law, so test it on your own task. The same page gives a rough guide: low for fast, well-scoped tasks, medium or high for complex changes and debugging, extra high for long, agentic, reasoning-heavy work. In Claude Code the same dial is slash effort.

Open-weight models are moving fast: Kimi, DeepSeek, GLM, and more every month. They are much cheaper per token, but cost per token is a head fake. In our own tests, open models were about a fifth of the price per token and about half the price per task, because they took more tokens and more turns. You can run them in the same harnesses: OpenCode out of the box, Codex with dash dash oss, or Claude Code pointed at a gateway. Own the weights, own the tradeoffs: you choose the host, the data policy, and the latency, and you also own the evals and the ops.

Both tools have two kinds of memory. The first is the file you just wrote: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Codex. You write it, you can read it, and it loads every session. And what ChatGPT remembers about you in the chat app doesn't carry over into Codex. Both vendors say the same thing: rules that must always apply go in the file. Automatic memory is a recall layer.

The full exercise
Now something technical, on purpose unfamiliar. Can two numbers in a list add up to ten? Interviewers call this Two Sum. Small problem. But we are building it as a real command inside a Valkey server, written in Rust. You do not need Rust or Valkey experience. That is the point: the agent does the parts you do not know, and you judge whether it actually works. What changes is how you verify: a module runs inside the server process, so a bug does not just fail a test, it can take the server down.

Rust Valkey module

What is Valkey?

An open-source, in-memory key-value store.
Keys hold strings, lists, sets, hashes
SET greeting hello→ OK
GET greeting→ hello
RPUSH demo:numbers 3 8 7→ 3
LRANGE demo:numbers 0 -1→ 3 8 7
Started in 2024 as a fork of Redis. Run by the Linux Foundation. Used for caching, queues, leaderboards.
The full exercise
Quick background for anyone who has not used it. Valkey is an open-source, in-memory key-value store. You send it commands: SET and GET a string, push numbers onto a list, read the list back. It started in 2024 as a fork of Redis, and it is run by the Linux Foundation. People use it for caching, queues, leaderboards, anything that needs to be fast. For this exercise, all you need is that a key can hold a list of numbers, and that everything is a command.
37 / 50
Rust Valkey module

What is a module?

A library the server loads to add new commands.
Load it at startup
valkey-server --loadmodule ./libvalkey_two_sum.so
Now the server has a new command
RPUSH demo:numbers 3 8 7→ 3
DEMO.HASPAIR demo:numbers→ 1
It runs inside the server process. Fast, and a crash takes the whole server down.
The full exercise
Valkey lets you add your own commands with modules. A module is a compiled library, a .so file on Linux, that the server loads when it starts. Once it is loaded, your command sits right next to the built-in ones, and any client can call it. We will write ours in Rust with the official SDK. The catch is that module code runs inside the server process. That makes it fast, with no network hop to the data. It also means a panic or a bad pointer does not just fail your command, it takes down the server and everyone using it. That is why the skill and the prompt are so strict.

The full exercise
The problem: do any two numbers in a list add up to ten? Three, eight, seven: three plus seven is ten, so the answer is one. One, two, four: nothing adds to ten, so zero. Watch the duplicates: a single five is not a pair, but two fives are. Interviewers call this Two Sum. We are not going to tell the agent how to solve it. It picks an approach, and in part three you ask it to make it faster, and measure whether it did.

Rules it can’t break
It runs inside ValkeyA crash takes the server down for everyone.
Compiling isn’t doneLoad it into a real Valkey and run the command.
PING proves nothingThe server answers PING even when your module failed to load.
The full exercise
This is the same idea as humanizer, for code. The skill is a short SKILL.md that routes to four references, and the agent reads only the ones the task needs. It does not contain the answer. It contains the hard-won rules: module code runs inside the server, so a panic kills the server. Build the smallest thing that loads before anything clever. Test against a real, disposable Valkey on loopback, never a server you care about. And never report success because it compiled or because PING answered.

Here is the prompt you paste in part one, drawn to scale by words. Look at where the words go. Only a handful say what to build. Far more say what it returns in the edge cases, what to do with bad input, and what must never happen: overflow must never wrap, a huge list is rejected before it is read, the list and its expiration never change. Then how to build it, how to make it reproducible, and the biggest block: how to prove it works, in a real, disposable Valkey. It ends with report honestly: do not claim success from a compile or a PING. Most of a good prompt is about failure, because that is where an agent guesses.

Review the behavior

Fresh session. Review before you fix.
At minimum
[5]0
[5, 5]1
[3, 7, "bad"]error, not an early 1
[-3, 13]error: no negatives
[264 − 1, 11]0, though 64-bit wrapping gives 10
a string keyWRONGTYPE

The full exercise
Start a fresh session and ask for a review before any fixes, ideally from a different model. These are the cases that catch real bugs: a single five is not a pair, two fives are. A bad value after an early match must still be an error, because the prompt says validate the whole list. The numbers are unsigned, so a negative number is an error, not a pair. And the overflow row: the largest unsigned 64-bit integer, and eleven. Together they really add up to two to the sixty-fourth plus ten, and in 64-bit math that wraps around to exactly ten. The answer must still be zero. Confirm each suspected defect against the prompt before fixing it, then add a regression test. A clean review is a fine result too.

More examples
Everything today was one prompt and one answer. Three tools take you past that. A goal keeps the agent going until a condition is true. In Claude Code, after every turn a separate, fresh model checks whether the condition holds, and if not, the agent takes another turn. Codex has the same idea, also called slash goal, with pause and resume. Here is one for the Valkey exercise: every case in the review table passes against the release module, or stop after twenty turns. Write it as something the agent can prove by running a command. Loop is different: it reruns a prompt on a schedule, like checking a deploy every five minutes. And workflows, in Claude Code, are a script that fans work out to many agents in a fixed order, like five parallel reviewers and then a verifier for every finding.
